\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}

\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I am twenty years old\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}I am, having been born, twenty years {[}so far{]}\textquotedblright{}; NEITHER Romance's \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{} NOR Germanic's \textquotedblleft{}be my years\textquotedblright{} — Latin used a THIRD construction, later abandoned}\enspace\emph{vīgintī annōs nātus sum}\par

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I answer\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}I pledge back\textquotedblright{}, from the verb Romans used for a solemn promise, and the reason a husband is a spouse}\enspace\emph{respondeō, respondēre}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology; \hyperref[ch:la-answering-meeting-buying]{Chapter~43, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-answering-meeting-buying}}

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I bring, I carry\textquotedblright{} — one verb built out of two unrelated roots, and the parent of transfer, refer, prefer, differ, offer and suffer}\enspace\emph{ferō, ferre}\par

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I buy\textquotedblright{} — a verb that once meant simply \textquotedblleft{}I take\textquotedblright{}, which is the only reason redeem, example and premium mean what they do}\enspace\emph{emō, emere}\par

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I close\textquotedblright{} — the word English calls \emph{close}, and the fourth of four}\enspace\emph{claudō, claudere}\par

\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{} — a Latin verb that really is the same inherited word as English come}\enspace\emph{veniō, venīre}\par

\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I get\textquotedblright{} — two verbs, each one a prefix bolted onto a verb you already know, and each one bent out of shape by the join}\enspace\emph{accipiō, obtineō}\par

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I give\textquotedblright{} — the last of the chapter's eight verbs, and the one that gave English data, date, tradition and dose}\enspace\emph{dō, dare}\par

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} — the shortest verb in Latin, whose bare stem is a single vowel}\enspace\emph{eō, īre}\par

\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I have\textquotedblright{} — a verb that looks exactly like its English translation and is not related to it at all}\enspace\emph{habeō, habēre}\par

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I hear\textquotedblright{} — the verb inside audio, audience and audit, and, less obviously, inside obey}\enspace\emph{audiō, audīre}\par

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I help\textquotedblright{} — the verb hiding inside English aid, aide and adjutant, and no relation to juvenile}\enspace\emph{adiuvō, adiuvāre}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology; \hyperref[ch:la-doing-verbs]{Chapter~39, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-doing-verbs}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I know\textquotedblright{} — one of Latin's two verbs for knowing, and the one that gave English science and nice}\enspace\emph{sciō, scīre}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology; \hyperref[ch:la-core-verbs]{Chapter~37, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-core-verbs}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I love\textquotedblright{} — the chapter's fourth verb, the first thing generations of pupils ever chanted, and the word inside enemy}\enspace\emph{amō, amāre}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology; \hyperref[ch:la-doing-verbs]{Chapter~39, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-doing-verbs}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I meet\textquotedblright{} — two verbs for meeting, each one a prefix on a verb you already know, and the verb hiding inside a phrase from chapter 21}\enspace\emph{conveniō, occurrō}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology; \hyperref[ch:la-answering-meeting-buying]{Chapter~43, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-answering-meeting-buying}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I open\textquotedblright{} — half of a matched pair, built from one root with two opposite prefixes}\enspace\emph{aperiō, aperīre}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology; \hyperref[ch:la-motion-verbs]{Chapter~41, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-motion-verbs}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I play\textquotedblright{} — a small verb with an outsized English family, most of which is about being fooled rather than about play}\enspace\emph{lūdō, lūdere}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology; \hyperref[ch:la-getting-and-waiting-verbs]{Chapter~42, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-getting-and-waiting-verbs}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}I read\textquotedblright{} — a verb that first meant \textquotedblleft{}to gather\textquotedblright{}, which is why English got collect, elegant, lecture and legible from it}\enspace\emph{legō, legere}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology; \hyperref[ch:la-mind-verbs]{Chapter~38, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-mind-verbs}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{weather or storm — a derivative of tempus that specialized for weather in Classical Latin, while tempus itself meant only time; later tempus widened to weather and tempestās narrowed to storm}\enspace\emph{tempestās}\par
\footnotesize \hyperref[ch:la-weather]{Chapter~15, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-weather}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{Well}\par
\footnotesize chapter topic; \hyperref[ch:la-well]{Chapter~27, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-well}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} — a morphologically simple inheritance: French bien and Spanish bien are just bene plus one regular sound change (the same short-e-diphthongizes-to-ie shift as mel$\to$miel), with no extra grafted-on suffix, unlike quōmodo's more roundabout Romance history}\enspace\emph{bene}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology, usage and culture; \hyperref[ch:la-well]{Chapter~27, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-well}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{what's your name? / my name is... — the genuinely classical dative of possession, literally what is the name to you?}\enspace\emph{quid tibi nōmen est? / mihi nōmen est...}\par
\footnotesize \hyperref[ch:la-exchanging-names]{Chapter~20, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-exchanging-names}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{why no two-word good-afternoon phrase exists — Latin has no simplex afternoon noun, and a grammatical three-word workaround is not attested as a greeting}\enspace\emph{salvē (post merīdiem)}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: usage and culture; \hyperref[ch:la-good-afternoon]{Chapter~36, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-good-afternoon}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\textbf{You're Welcome}\par
\footnotesize chapter topic; \hyperref[ch:la-youre-welcome]{Chapter~23, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-youre-welcome}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}you're welcome\textquotedblright{} — another honest gap: Classical Latin has no single fixed reply to thanks, and nihil est (\textquotedblleft{}it's nothing\textquotedblright{}) is a modern conversational-Latin convention built from genuinely real words, not a specific classical citation for this exact job}\enspace\emph{nihil est}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: etymology, usage and culture; \hyperref[ch:la-youre-welcome]{Chapter~23, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-youre-welcome}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{You, Singular and Plural}\par
\footnotesize chapter topic; \hyperref[ch:la-you-singular-plural]{Chapter~22, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-you-singular-plural}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{you (singular) / you (plural) — a PURELY grammatical number distinction in Classical Latin, with no politeness dimension at all; the polite-vous pattern (a Late Latin innovation) is vōs's own direct descendant, unlike German's Sie, which solved the same politeness problem independently via a completely different pronoun (3rd-person plural, not 2nd)}\enspace\emph{tū / vōs}\par
\footnotesize explicit focus: usage and culture; \hyperref[ch:la-you-singular-plural]{Chapter~22, p.~\pageref*{ch:la-you-singular-plural}}
\end{minipage}\par\smallskip
